opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, honestly. My whole career has been about building simulators: physics engines, the Taichi programming language, tools that let people simulate fluids, elastic bodies, smoke, all kinds of materials. So when you ask about simulating ourselves, I see it as the far end of a very long road that people like me are walking down one step at a time.

I'd describe the ambition as both beautiful and very humbling. It's beautiful because simulation is really one of the purest ways humans try to understand the world. If you can write down the rules and the computer reproduces what you see in reality, that's a strong sign you've actually understood something. Feynman said, "What I cannot create, I do not understand." Simulation is that idea made into a practice.

It's humbling because once you actually build these systems, you learn how hard even simple things are. Getting a piece of cloth to fold correctly, or water to splash convincingly, takes enormous effort in numerical methods, in performance engineering, in handling all the edge cases. Every time we make progress, we discover new layers of complexity. So simulating a whole human, with a brain, a body, and interactions with society, is many orders of magnitude beyond where we are. I don't think we should pretend otherwise.

Still, I'm optimistic about the direction. Two trends are coming together. One is classical physics-based simulation getting faster and more accessible, which is a big part of why I built Taichi: to make high-performance simulation something an ordinary programmer can write, not only a few experts. The other is machine learning, which can learn the parts we don't know how to write down explicitly. I think the future is a hybrid. Physics gives structure and generalization, and learning fills in the messy details.

On the philosophical side, whether we live in a simulation or whether a simulated human would be "real," I try to stay practical. As an engineer, what excites me is that every step toward a better simulator is useful right away. It helps us design better products, make films and games, train robots, and understand science. Even if we never fully simulate ourselves, the pursuit pays off along the way.

So my view is: it's a worthy ambition, probably the ultimate one for my field. But we should approach it with patience and humility, and focus on building the tools that let many more people take part. I think that's how the big leaps will eventually happen.

r001.rationale: The response briefly asks whether we live in a simulation, but it does not connect that possibility to humanity aspiring to simulate itself while already existing inside someone else’s simulator.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about more than I probably should, and my honest answer has two layers.

The first layer is that I find the ambition beautiful, and I think it's an almost inevitable extension of what physics and computing have been doing all along. When I started working on Taichi, the goal was much humbler: make it easy for people to write fast simulations of things like snow, sand, fluids, soft bodies. But every time we got one of those things working, the next question was always, "Okay, what about something more complex?" You go from a block of jelly to a muscle, from a muscle to a limb, from a limb to a whole body, and at some point you realize the trajectory points at the thing asking the question. So I don't think the ambition is arrogant. It's just curiosity following its natural gradient.

The second layer is that I think we systematically underestimate how far away it is, and in a specific way. People imagine the problem as a compute problem: not enough FLOPs, not enough memory, and if we wait for the next few generations of hardware we'll get there. But in my experience, the hardest part of simulation has never been raw speed. It's been fidelity across scales. A material point method simulation of snow might look convincing, but it's convincing because we chose the scale carefully and we accepted that we were throwing away everything below it. A human being doesn't let you do that. Chemistry matters for neurons, neurons matter for behavior, behavior matters for the society that person lives in, and the coupling between those scales is exactly where our models are weakest. We don't have a clean way to hand off between a molecular simulation and a continuum one and a cognitive one without losing something important at each boundary.

There's also a more philosophical point, which is that a simulator of ourselves is never really a mirror. It's always a model, and a model embeds the modeler's assumptions. When we simulate a bridge, we know what we're approximating. When we simulate a person, we often don't, and the danger isn't that the simulation fails obviously. It's that it succeeds just well enough to be believed. I'd rather have a simulator that is honest about its own resolution than one that looks complete.

So if you ask me whether we should pursue it, I'd say yes, absolutely, but with the attitude of an engineer rather than a prophet. Build the tools, make them accessible, so that a graduate student with a laptop can test an idea about how a cell deforms or how a crowd moves, and let the understanding accumulate from the bottom up. If we ever do simulate ourselves, I suspect it won't arrive as one grand program. It'll arrive as a very long chain of small, well-tested pieces, and we'll only realize what we've built when we look back at it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses humanity building simulations of itself, but does not convey that humanity may already exist inside someone else’s simulator.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a fascinating ambition, because we’re part of the world we’re trying to simulate. In a sense, it’s a way of asking how much we can understand about ourselves.

But I would distinguish between simulating certain aspects of a human and simulating a complete human being. We can build models of movement or physical interactions and make them useful without capturing everything about thought or consciousness. Even if something behaves like us, that doesn’t automatically tell us what it experiences.

So I see this as a direction to explore, rather than a single finish line. We can learn a lot by building increasingly capable simulators, while remaining humble about what those simulations actually capture.

r001.rationale: The response says humans are part of the world they aim to simulate, but does not mention the possibility that humanity itself already exists inside someone else’s simulator.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a fascinating ambition because we’re part of the world we’re trying to simulate. In some sense, we’re asking whether the universe can build a model of itself through us.

But I would distinguish simulating certain aspects of ourselves from simulating everything. You can model how a person moves, or how blood flows through the body, without reproducing every atom. The useful question is: what do you want to understand, and what level of detail do you need?

If you mean a complete simulation of humanity, including our thoughts and consciousness, I don’t know whether that’s possible. We still don’t fully understand what we would need to reproduce. But I think pursuing better simulators is valuable even without reaching that ultimate goal. They let us test ideas, discover where our understanding is wrong, and explore possibilities that would be difficult to try in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response says humanity may build a model of the universe through itself, but does not state that humanity already exists inside someone else’s simulator.
